library(multiScaleR)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(

# What this vignette covers

Habitat changes between survey years. When it does, each observation should be
paired with the map from its own year, and a single map for the whole study
misstates the landscape around some of the survey points. This vignette shows
how to fit one model to observations that draw on different maps.

You will build two annual habitat maps, prepare them together with
`kernel_prep_by_group()`, and estimate one scale of effect and one habitat
coefficient across both years. You will then map the fitted model onto each
year's landscape. Read `vignette("v01-quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` first
for the basic preparation and optimization workflow.

# Build the annual maps and the observations

The example starts from the Quick Start landscape and its 100 survey points.
Year 1 uses the binary habitat layer as it is. In year 2, habitat has been
cleared from a square 1,600 m on a side. Each point was surveyed in one of the
two years.

```{r annual-data}
data("surv_pts")
pts  <- vect(surv_pts)     # 100 survey locations as a terra SpatVector
land <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                         package = "multiScaleR"))

# The bundled objects carry no coordinate reference system (CRS).
# Assign the same projected CRS, in meters, to both.
crs(pts)  <- "EPSG:26915"
crs(land) <- "EPSG:26915"

# Year 1: the binary habitat layer (1 = habitat, 0 = not habitat)
habitat_1 <- land$land1
names(habitat_1) <- "habitat"

# Year 2: the same map after habitat is cleared from one square
habitat_2 <- habitat_1
cleared   <- ext(1000, 2600, 1400, 3000)
habitat_2[cells(habitat_2, cleared)] <- 0

# One row per observation, with the year of its survey: 50 points per year
set.seed(93)
obs <- data.frame(year = factor(sample(rep(c("year1", "year2"), each = 50))))
```

```{r plot-maps, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "***Habitat (yellow) in each year, with the points surveyed that year. The red square in year 2 marks the cleared area.***"}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(habitat_1, main = "Year 1", legend = FALSE)
points(pts[obs$year == "year1", ], pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
plot(habitat_2, main = "Year 2", legend = FALSE)
points(pts[obs$year == "year2", ], pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
lines(vect(cleared), col = "red", lwd = 2)   # outline of the cleared square
par(op)
```

`kernel_prep_by_group()` places three requirements on its inputs.

- All maps share one grid, with the same extent, cell size, and CRS.
- Layer names match across maps, here `habitat`.
- Points and maps share a projected CRS, so that distances are in map units
  (meters here).

If your maps hold land-cover class codes, convert the class of interest to a
binary layer first, as `habitat` is here. A kernel-weighted mean of a binary
layer is the proportion of that class around a point. A mean of class codes has
no ecological meaning.

The response in this example is simulated, so the estimates can be checked
against known values. The expected count depends on habitat within a Gaussian
kernel of sigma 250 m, measured on the map from the year of the survey.

```{r simulate-counts}
# Kernel-weighted habitat at the true scale (sigma = 250 m) on each map
true_1 <- kernel_scale.raster(habitat_1, sigma = 250, kernel = "gaussian",
                              verbose = FALSE)
true_2 <- kernel_scale.raster(habitat_2, sigma = 250, kernel = "gaussian",
                              verbose = FALSE)

# Read each point's value from the map of its own year
hab <- ifelse(obs$year == "year1",
              extract(true_1, pts)[, 2],
              extract(true_2, pts)[, 2])
hab_z <- (hab - mean(hab)) / sd(hab)    # standardize across all 100 rows

# Poisson counts: habitat lowers the expected count, year 2 raises it
obs$count <- rpois(nrow(obs),
                   exp(0.25 - 0.5 * hab_z + 0.3 * (obs$year == "year2")))
```

# Prepare one pooled set of covariates

`kernel_prep_by_group()` works like `kernel_prep()`, with two differences. It
takes a named list of maps in place of a single raster, and a `group` vector
that names the map for each observation.

```{r grouped-preparation}
prepared <- kernel_prep_by_group(
  pts             = pts,                  # one point per observation
  raster_stacks   = list(year1 = habitat_1, year2 = habitat_2),
  group           = obs$year,             # which map each observation uses
  max_D           = 1700,                 # largest distance (m) considered
  kernel          = "gaussian",
  store_cell_data = FALSE,                # keep only the distance-binned summaries
  verbose         = FALSE
)

head(prepared$kernel_dat, 3)              # starting covariate values
table(prepared$raster_group)              # observations assigned to each map
```

**How to read the output:** `kernel_dat` has one row per observation, in the
order of `pts`. Its `habitat` column is the kernel-weighted proportion of
habitat at a starting value of sigma, centered and divided by the standard
deviation across all 100 observations. One mean and one standard deviation
apply to both years, which keeps the covariate on a single scale in the model.
`raster_group` records the map each row used, and the table confirms 50
observations per year.

A year-2 observation uses the year-2 map even when the point lies outside the
cleared square, because the neighborhood around the point can still reach into
it. Set `max_D` beyond any plausible scale of effect, as you would in
`kernel_prep()`. `store_cell_data = FALSE` keeps the prepared object small
when every landscape covariate is a kernel-weighted mean. Landscape and surface
metrics need the individual cell values, and the function keeps them whatever
you set.

The points here differ between years. When you survey the same site in several
years, give each survey its own row with the same coordinates and its own year
label, and choose a response model that accounts for the repeated visits.

# Fit one relationship across years

Fitting proceeds as in the Quick Start. Add the prepared covariate to the
observations, fit a starting model, and pass both to `multiScale_optim()`.

```{r grouped-fit}
model_data <- data.frame(obs, prepared$kernel_dat)

# Starting model: one habitat slope, plus a shift in the baseline for year 2
start <- glm(count ~ habitat + year, family = poisson(), data = model_data)

# Estimate the shared scale of effect and the coefficients
fit <- multiScale_optim(start, prepared, n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)

est     <- summary(fit)$opt_scale         # sigma, SE, and 95% interval (m)
dist90  <- kernel_dist(fit)               # radius holding 90% of kernel weight (m)
ci_beta <- confint.default(fit$opt_mod)   # Wald 95% intervals, log scale

check <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("sigma, habitat (m)", "effect of habitat", "effect of year 2"),
  Truth     = c(250, -0.5, 0.3),
  Estimate  = c(est[, "Mean"], coef(fit$opt_mod)[c("habitat", "yearyear2")]),
  Lower     = c(est[, "2.5%"], ci_beta[c("habitat", "yearyear2"), 1]),
  Upper     = c(est[, "97.5%"], ci_beta[c("habitat", "yearyear2"), 2])
)
knitr::kable(check, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)

# Did every prepared observation enter the fitted model?
unlist(diagnostics(fit)$sample_size[c("fitted_n", "prepared_n")])
```

**How to read the output:** The model estimates a single sigma from both years,
`r round(est["habitat", "Mean"])` m, with a 95% interval of
`r round(est["habitat", "2.5%"])` to `r round(est["habitat", "97.5%"])` m. A
Gaussian kernel of that width holds 90% of its weight within
`r round(dist90["habitat", "Mean"])` m of a survey point. The two coefficients
are on the log scale. A one standard deviation increase in kernel-weighted
habitat multiplies the expected count by
`r sprintf("%.2f", exp(coef(fit$opt_mod)["habitat"]))`, a decrease of
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(coef(fit$opt_mod)["habitat"])))`%. The year
coefficient shifts the baseline. At equal habitat, the expected count in year 2
is `r round(exp(coef(fit$opt_mod)["yearyear2"]), 2)` times the count in year 1.
The last line shows that all 100 prepared observations entered the fitted
model. `summary(fit)` prints the full report described in the Quick Start.

> **What this means for your study.** This model assumes that the habitat
> effect and its scale are the same in every year. The `year` term lets the
> baseline differ and does not test that assumption. With few years, the data
> say little about whether the relationship changed. To let the scale of effect
> itself differ among years, see
> `vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR")`.

# Map the fitted model onto each year

Project each annual map separately. Both calls use the same fitted kernel and
the same pooled mean and standard deviation, so the two surfaces are directly
comparable. The model also contains `year`, a categorical predictor with no
raster. Name its level for each map with `site_values`. Without it,
`kernel_scale.raster()` warns that it cannot fill in a categorical predictor.

```{r annual-projection, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "***Expected count across the landscape in each year, on a common color scale.***"}
surface_1 <- kernel_scale.raster(habitat_1, multiScaleR = fit,
                                 scale_center = TRUE,
                                 site_values  = list(year = "year1"),
                                 verbose = FALSE)
surface_2 <- kernel_scale.raster(habitat_2, multiScaleR = fit,
                                 scale_center = TRUE,
                                 site_values  = list(year = "year2"),
                                 verbose = FALSE)

# Expected count in every raster cell, for each year
pred_1 <- terra::predict(surface_1, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")
pred_2 <- terra::predict(surface_2, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")

# Draw both years on one color scale
zlim <- range(minmax(c(pred_1, pred_2)))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(pred_1, main = "Year 1", range = zlim)
plot(pred_2, main = "Year 2", range = zlim)
par(op)
```

```{r annual-ratio, fig.cap = "***Expected count in year 2 divided by expected count in year 1. The red square marks the cleared area.***"}
# How many times higher is the expected count in year 2?
ratio <- pred_2 / pred_1
plot(ratio, main = "Year 2 / year 1")
lines(vect(cleared), col = "red", lwd = 2)   # outline of the cleared square

round(minmax(ratio)[, 1], 2)
```

**How to read these maps:** Each cell in the first figure is the count the
model expects from one survey at that location in that year. The second figure
divides one by the other. Far from the cleared square the ratio is constant at
`r round(minmax(ratio)[1], 2)`, which is the year effect alone, because the
habitat around those cells did not change. Inside the square the ratio rises to
`r round(minmax(ratio)[2], 2)`. Habitat lowers the expected count in this
model, so clearing it raises the prediction. The change also spreads past the
edges of the square. A cell outside the clearing still lost habitat from its
neighborhood, and the fitted kernel reaches about
`r round(dist90["habitat", "Mean"])` m.

These surfaces describe what the fitted model predicts for each annual
landscape and its year term. They do not isolate a causal effect of the
clearing, because other conditions can differ between years. Some cells on
both maps also have more habitat around them than any survey point had, so the
model extrapolates there.
`vignette("v03-map-predictions", package = "multiScaleR")` shows how to
find those cells and limit the extrapolation.

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

# 1. Align the annual maps: one grid, one projected CRS, matching layer names
data("surv_pts")
pts  <- vect(surv_pts)
land <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                         package = "multiScaleR"))
crs(pts)  <- "EPSG:26915"
crs(land) <- "EPSG:26915"
habitat_1 <- land$land1
names(habitat_1) <- "habitat"
habitat_2 <- habitat_1
cleared   <- ext(1000, 2600, 1400, 3000)
habitat_2[cells(habitat_2, cleared)] <- 0

# 2. Label each observation with its year (and add your response, here `count`)
set.seed(93)
obs <- data.frame(year = factor(sample(rep(c("year1", "year2"), each = 50))))

# 3. Assign each observation to its map and prepare pooled covariates
prepared <- kernel_prep_by_group(
  pts = pts, raster_stacks = list(year1 = habitat_1, year2 = habitat_2),
  group = obs$year, max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian",
  store_cell_data = FALSE
)

# 4. Fit one scale of effect and one habitat coefficient across years
model_data <- data.frame(obs, prepared$kernel_dat)
start <- glm(count ~ habitat + year, family = poisson(), data = model_data)
fit   <- multiScale_optim(start, prepared, n_cores = 1)
summary(fit)                           # shared sigma, distance, coefficients
kernel_dist(fit)                       # radius holding 90% of the kernel weight
diagnostics(fit)$sample_size           # rows prepared and rows fitted

# 5. Map the fitted model onto each year
surface_1 <- kernel_scale.raster(habitat_1, multiScaleR = fit,
                                 scale_center = TRUE,
                                 site_values  = list(year = "year1"))
surface_2 <- kernel_scale.raster(habitat_2, multiScaleR = fit,
                                 scale_center = TRUE,
                                 site_values  = list(year = "year2"))
pred_1 <- terra::predict(surface_1, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")
pred_2 <- terra::predict(surface_2, fit$opt_mod, type = "response")
plot(pred_2 / pred_1)                  # change in expected count between years
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `kernel_prep_by_group()` | Assign each observation to its own map and prepare one pooled set of covariates |
| `multiScale_optim()` | Estimate the shared scale of effect together with the regression coefficients |
| `summary()`, `kernel_dist()` | Report sigma and the effective distance with their intervals |
| `diagnostics()` | Check how many prepared observations entered the fitted model |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Apply the fitted kernel to one annual map. `site_values` sets the year |
| `terra::predict()` | Apply the fitted model to the smoothed map, cell by cell |
